figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: A map of the perspective paper. Part I says why the era of Physical AI holds a second form of intelligent individual, the person augmented by AI, and what a cognitive symbiont is. Part II follows one loop, in which the output of each section is the input of the next, with a runtime beneath it and trust around it. Part III widens the view from one augmented individual to many. Part IV examines the risks, how augmentation can be governed, and how the whole can be measured. Each box names the section’s purpose and the figures, tables, and equations it contributes.
figures.headline: Four parts map the paper, with Part II a single loop of sections in which each output becomes the next section's input.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 lays them out.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The two halves of the endgame. AGI runs from chatbots to autonomous agents and is scored on what the AI completes. AHI runs from reactive assistants to cognitive symbionts and is scored on what the person can now do. Both share one base of models, agents, memory, and hardware, and both inherit every improvement to it. A system sits on one half or the other according to what it is evaluated on, so the same chat product is a chatbot when its answers are scored and a reactive assistant when what its user can then do is scored; today the first two stages of the AHI half are still scored on what the AI produces (Table 1). Arrows mark growth within a half, and the two halves are parallel, not successive stages.
figures.headline: Both halves share one model base, but AGI is scored on what the AI completes and AHI on what the person can now do.
citing_sentences: What differs is the object of evaluation, the mode of existence, and the relationship with the person (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: (a) AI capability on isolated tasks keeps rising while coupling with a particular person stays nearly flat; the shaded region is augmentation that is never realized. The curves are a conceptual sketch, not measurements. (b) The mechanism of the shift: a causal loop in which stronger base models lower the cost of being understood, move interaction onto the body, and generate a new kind of context that makes the models more useful to each person in turn, without being used to train them.
figures.headline: A conceptual sketch shows AI capability rising while its coupling with a particular person stays nearly flat.
citing_sentences: The result is a widening gap between what a model could contribute and what a person actually receives (Figure 3a).

Figure 3b shows the mechanism by which the relationship nonetheless shifts: stronger models absorb more context, which lowers the cost of being understood, which moves interaction off the screen and onto the body, which produces a new kind of context, the record of a life, which makes those models more useful to that person in turn.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Two forms of intelligent individuals. Left: an AI-augmented individual, a person with a symbiont that senses and speaks through wearable devices. Middle: an AI as individual, an embodied robot. The two share one cognitive core, indicated by the common bar. Right, in lighter tone: devices in the environment that either form can reach into (Section 14.2). The paper’s scope is the left form. “AI as individual” is a functional description and carries no claim about consciousness or legal personhood.
figures.headline: Two forms of intelligent individual share one cognitive core, and the paper addresses only the augmented-person form.
citing_sentences: On the horizontal axis, we foresee, there are two ways for an intelligent individual to exist in the future world of Physical AI (Figure 4).
The third column of Figure 4, AI-driven devices in the environment, appears in the paper only as the symbiont’s extended reach into the physical world (Section 14.2).
This section scales the symbiont from one person to a society and returns to the full picture of Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: The stack a symbiont is built on. From the bottom: wearable and embedded hardware, foundation models (one axis that runs from language to omni-modal to reasoning to world models), the personal runtime, the agentic harness, and the symbiont layer that this paper proposes. The side notes record what exists today and what the paper adds at each level.
figures.headline: A symbiont layer sits at the top of a stack built on hardware, foundation models, a personal runtime, and an agentic harness.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows how the five lines stack up and where the layer this paper proposes sits.
This is the layer that, in the stack of Figure 5, sits between the foundation models and the agentic harness, and that may in time grow into an AI-native operating system.
Figure 17 expands the upper part of Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: The symbiosis loop. Six stages run around the person; the runtime beneath them makes the loop run across devices and time, and trust encloses everything. The person’s own words enter the record directly. Silence is drawn as a formal output, and acting for and thinking with share one stage.
figures.headline: Six stages surround the person in one loop, with a runtime beneath it and trust enclosing everything.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 is the map of the research space and the table of contents of Part II.
The loop of Figure 6 opens with the question of what the symbiont senses the person with and what it speaks to them through.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: The device constellation. Each device carries a role on the way in (sensing, private input) or on the way out (private output, shared canvas), and often both; a runtime manages them as a single set of senses. The symbiont itself has no body and borrows every one of them. Neural interfaces and the devices of the environment are the far end of the constellation.
figures.headline: A constellation of wearables and devices gives one symbiont its senses and outputs, managed by a single runtime.
citing_sentences: No single device can carry all of this, so a symbiont senses and speaks through a constellation (Figure 7): glasses with a first-person camera, microphones, eye tracking, and a one-line display; a pendant or pin that records audio and takes snapshots all day and stands in when glasses are not worn; earbuds or bone conduction for private voice output; a microphone close to the mouth so that the person can speak to it at the level of a breath without being overheard; a ring, watch, or band for heart rate, sleep, and activity, and increasingly for EMG gestures; a phone for compute and a screen on the move; and a desktop with authorized access to screen content, the IDE, documents, and meeting software.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Three timescales of one record. Live context is large and mostly discarded, working state holds projects and open threads for days to weeks, and knowledge is small, curated, and persistent. Consolidation moves material up; recall moves the right slice down into the working context $c_{t}$ of Definition 4.1.
figures.headline: Live context is large and mostly discarded, while knowledge is small and persistent, with consolidation and recall between them.
citing_sentences: Two flows connect the three layers (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: One life, many views. The same handful of events (a meeting, a family plan, a bad night’s sleep) appears in six views, by logic, domain, person, lifetime, time, and nature. The views are projections of one record and can be switched at will.
figures.headline: The same handful of events appears in six views, each projected from one record and switchable at will.
citing_sentences: The organizing claim of the section is that the same record is projected into different views depending on the question, and that any view can be switched to at any time (Figure 9, Table 8).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Two roads to the mind. Observation infers patterns from behavior and physiology; self-report records what the person says about intent, feeling, and reasons. Both feed one layered model, with every entry tagged by source and uncertainty; disagreements are marked, down-weighted, and resolved by asking.
figures.headline: Observation and self-report feed one layered model, with disagreements marked, down-weighted, and resolved by asking.
citing_sentences: There are two independent sources of evidence about a mind, and a symbiont needs both (Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Two axes of the backbone. Columns: the family of foundation models, from language to sight and sound to dynamics, each extending what counts as evidence. Rows: how much system is organized around the model, from a single pass to a process inside an agentic harness. The two axes are independent, since a harness can be wrapped around any of the three models; the dashed path is the likely order in which systems will move through the grid, and the heavy line is the information interface of the personal model, which is the same in every cell.
figures.headline: A six-cell grid crosses three kinds of foundation model with harness organization, so the two axes vary independently.
citing_sentences: Two independent axes describe the engine (Figure 11).
The grid of Figure 11 therefore has six cells, and the two axes can be traversed independently.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Cognitive full-duplex. One exchange in a team meeting: a colleague raises a figure the person reported last quarter, the slow loop retrieves and checks it, the fast loop places a one-line cue in the glasses within a second, the person answers, and the cue is withdrawn once it expires. The timeline below follows the exchange across the four tracks of the external world, outward expression, the private channel, and the symbiont’s internal state. The help is a reminder of the person’s own figure, the kind of assistance most settings accept (Section 15.5), and most of the time the right output is silence.
figures.headline: A fast cue appears in the glasses within a second during a meeting, then is withdrawn once it expires.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 shows one instance.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: The ladder of assistance. Tier 1 is where today’s agents stop; a symbiont does the same tasks with the person’s context in hand. Tier 2 is thinking and feeling with the person, and Tier 3 is living among others. The depth of the personal model required grows with each tier, and caring runs across all three.
figures.headline: Three tiers of assistance rise from getting tasks done to thinking and feeling with the person to living among others.
citing_sentences: The answer is a ladder with three tiers (Figure 13).

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: The symbiont handshake. Four rings of authorization around each person, from visible to committable; exchange happens only within the ring both have opened, and the inner model never crosses.
figures.headline: Four rings of authorization govern when two symbionts may exchange information, and the inner model never crosses.
citing_sentences: It is at once fanciful and practical, and Figure 14 turns it into four research questions.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: The learning spectrum. The lower band runs from changing only memory to changing all parameters; each mechanism is rated for the data it needs, its stability, and its reversibility, and the paper argues for the middle-left region. The upper band is harness-level learning, which runs in parallel, stays readable and reversible, and is where self-improvement should mostly happen.
figures.headline: A learning spectrum runs from changing only memory to changing all parameters, with the favored region toward the middle-left.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 arranges the parameter-side mechanisms on one axis from changing only memory to changing all parameters, rates each for the data it needs, its stability, and its reversibility, and adds a parallel band for the harness.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Co-evolution of a person and a stack. Above the axis, events in the person’s life; below it, changes in the system: base model upgrades, routines and skills the harness accumulates, new hardware. Dashed links show life events triggering system learning and system changes altering what is observed next. The heavy line is the record and personal model, the one thing never replaced. In the fiction, the counterpart of this growth is Jarvis’s cognitive core eventually gaining a body as the Vision (Section 14.2), and the counterexample is Ultron, a separate project whose goals diverged from its maker’s (Section 15.7).
figures.headline: Life events and system changes alternate over time, while the record and personal model stay fixed as the one thing never replaced.
citing_sentences: As understanding of the person deepens, the base model, the harness, and the hardware must all evolve, along three routes that share one set of constraints (Figure 16).

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: The personal runtime. Base capabilities can be swapped freely; the record and personal model at the top are never swapped. The harness gets things done; the runtime puts them on the right device, with the right permission, at the right time. The trust layer runs through everything.
figures.headline: Swappable base capabilities sit beneath a record and personal model that are never swapped, with the harness and runtime between them.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 expands the upper part of Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: The trust curve. Data authorization (solid, read on the left axis) and action permission (dashed, read on the right axis) climb in steps as time together and delivered value accumulate. Each data level names what must be proved before the next is opened, each action level is earned a little after the data level it needs, and a breach sends authorization back one step. The system has to be useful at the lowest level already.
figures.headline: Data authorization and action permission rise in steps as time together grows, and a breach sends authorization back one step.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 plots authorization against time together and value delivered.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: A map of beneficiaries. Horizontal: how much of a population’s gap a symbiont can close today (observability times closability). Vertical: the size and stakes of the gap. Bubble size is population; color is the maturity of the evidence. Positions are the author’s judgments, not measurements.
figures.headline: A map places populations by the size of their gap and how much of it can be closed, with positions that are author judgments.
citing_sentences: Figure 19 maps populations on two of these dimensions, the size and stakes of the gap and how much of it can be closed today (observability times closability), with bubble size for population and color for the maturity of the evidence; feasibility is argued in the text, and the rest of the section argues each bubble.
Older adults sit in the upper right of Figure 19.

The position of the paper is to enter through support and early recognition and never through treatment, to make the handoff to professionals part of the function, and to place people in serious distress in the upper left of Figure 19: a large gap that cannot be closed first.

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: Three directions of harm around an augmented person, and their sum at the scale of a society. Harm to the person comes from the system, its provider, or an attacker; harm through the person reaches the people and institutions the person deals with; harm from institutions comes from those that deploy the paradigm for their own ends. Chips name the risks, and section marks point to where each is treated.
figures.headline: Three directions of harm around an augmented person add up at the scale of a society, with each risk named on the chart.
citing_sentences: Harm runs in three directions around an augmented person, and at the scale of a society the three add up to a collective harm (Figure 20).

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: From components to a life. Six stages of accumulating capability, the evidence that would justify moving to the next, and the open problems of Table 18 mapped onto them.
figures.headline: Six stages of accumulating capability, each with evidence required before advancing and open problems mapped onto it.
citing_sentences: Figure 21 orders capabilities in six stages, from a streaming cognitive copilot on the desktop with Tier 1 by delegation, to a persistent record and model, to the device constellation, to private input, to lifelong co-adaptation, and to networks of symbionts, with the evidence needed to move from each stage to the next and the open problems mapped onto them.

abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

sections.body: The section argues that current AI is judged by what a machine accomplishes on its own, while ordinary losses remain: forgotten knowledge, missed details, failed recall, and missing support. It describes a researcher whose idea slips away, whose published figure she cannot recall, and whose past reasoning is lost. The authors propose a second half of the endgame, AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. The paper's contribution is the framing, the design space, and the standard of evidence, not a new algorithm. Risks such as covert assistance in examinations are treated as part of the proposal.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: AI progress is scored by what machines do alone, leaving everyday losses of memory and support unaddressed.

sections.body: Table 1 divides human–AI relations into four roles: reactive assistant, autonomous agent, personal agent, and cognitive symbiont. Across the roles, the AI knows more, sits closer to the person, and offers value that shifts from information toward making the person more capable. Table 2 places the paper in a lineage from Licklider (1960) and Engelbart (1962) to 2026 personal agent products. The authors state a narrow claim: none of these lines takes the augmentation of a particular person across a life as its target. The section also lists five conditions that make the problem tractable now.
sections.heading: 2 Where We Stand
sections.headline: Prior work on human–AI roles and augmentation has not targeted augmenting one particular person across a life.

sections.body: The section reads five technology lines for what each provides and what each lacks: foundation models, agents and harnesses, memory and context, world models, and wearable hardware. Foundation models give a brain for language, images, and sound, but have no persistence, no sense of time, and no body. Agents give hands, but they are task-level and request-driven, with no senses and no model of the person. Memory systems remember dialogue rather than a life, and their personalization optimizes for sounding like the person. Table 3 maps each gap to the sections that address it. The section reports no benchmark numbers.
sections.heading: 3 Technical Foundations
sections.headline: Five existing technology lines supply most parts a symbiont needs, but none targets augmenting one particular person.

sections.body: The section defines the cognitive gap as the invariant of the paper: the price a person pays in what they forgot, failed to notice, could not think through, or could not put into words. A symbiont aims to shrink this gap by returning the relevant part of the person's own context at the right moment. Six properties are required: lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive. The properties pull against one another, for example proactive against low-friction. Section 4.4 lists non-claims, including that the symbiont does not read thoughts that were never expressed.
sections.heading: 4 Conceptual Foundations
sections.headline: The paper defines a cognitive gap, six required properties, and a symbiosis loop that organizes its design space.

sections.body: A symbiont has no body of its own, so it borrows senses from a constellation of devices: glasses with a first-person camera, microphones, a pendant, earbuds, a ring or band, a phone, and a desktop. Table 5 lists signal sources and what each reveals about the physical and mental sides of a life. Output uses private channels such as in-ear voice, a line on the glasses, and haptics, with strength matched to the setting. The section states that the content of an exchange stays with the person, while discreet delivery is a capability whose use follows the setting. Always-on operation means availability, not full computation, and is managed by a cognitive duty cycle.
sections.heading: 5 Sensing and Interacting
sections.headline: A symbiont must borrow its senses and voice from wearable devices, favoring private input and private output.

sections.body: The section separates three timescales in one record: live context, which is large and mostly discarded; working state, which lasts days or weeks; and knowledge, which is small, curated, and persistent. Consolidation moves material upward, and recall moves relevant knowledge back into the current context. Table 7 shows that each source, such as a chatbot, coding environment, or wearable, sees only part of a person, so one entry point must receive every source, with each source authorized separately. Views such as logic, domain, and lifetime are projections of the same record. The section also states that deleting a raw record does not delete the summaries derived from it.
sections.heading: 6 Personal Context and Lifelong Knowledge
sections.headline: Context, working state, and knowledge form one record across three timescales, fed by one entry point for all sources.

sections.body: The section defines what must be understood: the situation, the mind, and change over time. Evidence arrives by two roads. The observation road infers from behavior and physiology, while the self-report road records what the person says, and every entry carries its source and uncertainty. Table 9 gives seven layers, from stable identity to preferences about help, each with its evidence, rate of change, and typical misuse. The backbone is treated as replaceable, with language, omni-modal, and world models as one family. The section explicitly excludes reading thoughts that were never expressed, and it notes that familiarity with a person is not competence on the problem they face.
sections.heading: 7 Understanding a Person
sections.headline: The personal model fuses observation with self-report across seven layers, on any backbone, and declares its own limits.

sections.body: The section turns presence into mechanisms. A fast loop handles immediate cues, such as a name or a number, using small models on the device, while a slow loop retrieves and prepares material in the background. Table 10 separates three decisions: what to help with, when, and how. Silence is always an available answer, and the default when unsure. The paper gives a constrained choice in which the confidence threshold rises with the intrusiveness of an action, and it leaves the weights as research variables with no numerical values. The section also treats the person's attention as a budget to be managed, like battery charge.
sections.heading: 8 Living Alongside
sections.headline: A fast loop and a slow loop let the symbiont speak privately at the right moment, with silence as a formal choice.

sections.body: The section arranges assistance in three tiers. The first gets things done by delegating to standard agents while keeping the task definition, personal defaults, and decisions about when to consult the person. Table 11 compares an agent that must be told details with a symbiont that already knows them, measured by clarifying questions and corrections. The second tier thinks and feels with the person, covering decisions, goal formation, metacognition, tutoring, and everyday steadiness. The third tier lives among others. The section proposes five levels of action permission, from look to execute what cannot be undone, and states that a draft never becomes an outward commitment on its own.
sections.heading: 9 The Ladder of Assistance
sections.headline: Assistance is organized in three tiers, from completing tasks to thinking with the person to living among others.

sections.body: The section lists seven places where a symbiont can learn, from the record and personal model to model parameters, harness, hardware, and the person. It presents a personal data flywheel as a research hypothesis with two brakes. The first is echo: the system may read the effects of its own influence as a trait of the person, so each update must take the system's action as an argument. The second is validation, since more data does not guarantee a truer understanding. The section requires that a change of base model, harness, or hardware preserve the relationship. It also cites a randomized study in which three of six observed interaction patterns preserved learning.
sections.heading: 10 Growing Together
sections.headline: The symbiont and the person change together, and each model update must account for the system's own actions.

sections.body: The section argues that a symbiont needs persistent state across devices, one permission model, scheduling of several senses and outputs, management of the two loops, and one entry point for every context. These requirements exceed any single application and fall short of a new kernel. Figure 17 shows a stack in which base capabilities can be swapped while the record and personal model are never swapped. On cost, the section says that most of the time a lightweight model only detects events, and a heavier model runs when events occur. Continuity across devices, interruptions, and upgrades is the runtime's central duty, and after a gap the system does not pretend it was present.
sections.heading: 11 The Personal Runtime
sections.headline: A personal runtime spanning devices and applications is needed, since no single application can hold continuity.

sections.body: The section treats trust as part of the design rather than a later addition. Data authorization climbs in steps, from desktop and text to voice, first-person sight and sound, physiology, and the private channel, and each step must be earned. Three principles govern tiered access: the system must be useful at every level, data from a higher level is not used automatically for a lower-level task, and processing stays local by preference. Table 14 sets out nine design principles, including that a symbiont must be pausable, correctable, and leavable. The section states that verifiability and tamper evidence replace any aim of being unbreakable.
sections.heading: 12 Trust
sections.headline: Trust is treated as architecture: authorization climbs in steps, and the system must be useful at low authorization.

sections.body: The section argues who gains using four criteria: the size of the gap, its observability, its closability by the functions of Table 12, and the feasibility of channels and trust. Knowledge workers come first because they are the easiest group on which to verify the approach. Older adults and people with sensory, motor, cognitive, or language barriers gain the most per person, and everyday life gives the largest total gain. Children with all-day sensing of their own, people in acute crisis with a symbiont as their only support, and anyone in a compelled setting should not come first. Table 15 summarizes each population, and the placements in Figure 19 are the author's judgments.
sections.heading: 13 Whom It Serves
sections.headline: Knowledge workers come first to verify the approach, while children, acute crisis cases, and compelled settings should wait.

sections.body: The section is the most speculative part of the paper. It describes a future street where a researcher's morning idea is filed under its project, a figure is recalled in a meeting, a trip is booked without a question, and a fitting sentence follows a failure. The authors state that the scene presupposes the functions of Part II, and that its date depends on open problems rather than a single breakthrough. On robots, the section makes one claim: embodied intelligence needs a cognitive core of this kind as much as a better body. It also names a cost, since every moment of help is also a moment of sensing, and bystanders without a symbiont appear in the records of others.
sections.heading: 14 A World of Augmented Individuals
sections.headline: In a speculative street scene, every person is augmented, and augmented people and embodied robots share one cognitive core.

sections.body: The section names four features that change the risks of augmentation: attribution, invisibility, reach, and position. Position matters because gains are often relative, so one person's augmentation can be another's loss and can pressure everyone to adopt. Harm is sorted into three directions: to the person, through the person to others, and from institutions. The section cites a study in which a chatbot built on a language model induced more than three times as many false memories as a control condition. It also cites a survey of more than ten thousand US adults, in which a majority judged cognition-improving brain implants a bad idea for society. Table 16 lists, for each function, the settings where it is contested and the default the paper proposes.
sections.heading: 15 The Risks of Augmentation
sections.headline: Augmentation creates risks beyond the system: attribution, invisibility, reach into others' lives, and pressure to adopt.

sections.body: The section argues that a symbiont can follow the rules of the settings a person enters, because it is external, removable, and inspectable. The governing principle separates private content from declarable status: the content of an exchange stays private, while the presence of assistance is declared where a setting asks. Four assistance policies run from unassisted to full assistance. Verifiable abstention, a proof that a device kept a policy without revealing its record, is listed as an open problem. The section admits that such a proof cannot show that a person carried no second device. Governance runs on five layers of design, norms, law, markets, and research, and the paper proposes law for none of them.
sections.heading: 16 Governing Augmentation
sections.headline: Symbionts would follow declared assistance policies, though proving abstention remains an open problem alongside norms and law.

sections.body:
Section 17 replaces measuring the AI with measuring the person. Augmentation is the gain of the person with the symbiont over the person alone, Eq. (2). Three further quantities complete it:

- **Synergy** asks whether the pair beats the better of the two alone.
- **Retention** asks whether the person is stronger after the symbiont is removed.
- **The personalization differential** compares the same base model with and without personal context.

Table 17 lists ten dimensions, each paired with what it cannot establish alone. The section names four layers of method, with N-of-1 and longitudinal designs as primary and at least three baselines. It notes that learning effects can confound crossovers and that long-term studies must report the people who left.
sections.heading: 17 Evaluation and Research Agenda
sections.headline: Success is measured by the person's unaided gain, not the AI's output, across ten dimensions and four study designs.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the paper's case for AI-augmented human intelligence and names the cognitive symbiont as its form. A symbiont is lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive. It is built on foundation models, agents and their harnesses, memory and context engineering, world models, and wearable hardware.

The symbiont climbs a ladder from doing the person's errands, to thinking a problem through with them, to holding them steady among other people. Evaluation changes accordingly, to augmentation, synergy, and retention. The three largest blank regions are the evidence on which a mind can be modeled, the timing of participation, and the stability of learning and evolution over a life. The heaviest region is governance in settings where people compete and trust one another.
sections.heading: 18 Conclusion
sections.headline: A lifelong personal companion should be judged by what the person can do, and three regions of the map remain blank.
